hook: Chemists have measured the enthalpy of maybe a few thousand reactions directly, yet you can find ΔH for millions. The trick: measure one number per compound, the energy of making it from its elements, and let every reaction pass through the elements on paper.

prereq.why: The energy flows the other way, so ΔH has the same size and opposite sign.

figure.caption: Every reaction can be routed through the elements: take the reactants apart, then build the products. Only ΔH°f values are needed.

chain.cause: ΔH°f is the enthalpy change to make 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states
chain.effect: each compound gets one tabulated number; elements in their standard states get zero

chain.cause: A reaction can be imagined as reactants → elements → products
chain.effect: taking reactants apart costs −Σ ΔH°f(reactants); building products costs +Σ ΔH°f(products)

chain.cause: The route does not change the overall enthalpy change
chain.effect: ΔH°rxn = Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants)

chain.cause: ΔH°f values are measured for each substance and state
chain.effect: the result is more exact than a bond-enthalpy estimate

ideas: The standard enthalpy of formation, ΔH°f, is ΔH for making 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states (most stable form at 1 atm, usually 25 °C).
ΔH°f = 0 for an element in its standard state: O₂(g), H₂(g), C(graphite), Br₂(l), Fe(s).
ΔH°rxn = Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants): products minus reactants, each times its coefficient.
States matter: H₂O(l) −285.8 and H₂O(g) −241.8 kJ/mol.
Bond enthalpies: broken − formed. Formation: products − reactants. Do not mix them up.

misconception.wrong: Every pure substance made of one element, like O₃ or O atoms, has ΔH°f = 0.
misconception.right: Only the standard state, the most stable form at 1 atm and 25 °C, has ΔH°f = 0. O₂(g) is zero; O₃(g) and O(g) are positive.

summary: A standard enthalpy of formation is ΔH for making 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states; elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0. Any reaction's ΔH° is the sum of ΔH°f of the products minus the sum for the reactants, each multiplied by its coefficient.
